description_full: Oppenheimer Holdings Inc. operates as a middle-market investment bank and full-service broker-dealer. It provides brokerage services covering corporate equity and debt securities, money market instruments, exchange-traded options, municipal bonds, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, certain precious metals, and unit investment trusts; financial and wealth planning services; and margin lending services. The company also offers asset management services, including separately managed accounts, mutual fund managed accounts, discretionary portfolio management programs, non-discretionary investment advisory and consultation services, alternative investments, portfolio enhancement programs, and institutional taxable fixed income portfolio management strategies and solutions, as well as taxable and non-taxable fixed income portfolios and strategies. In addition, it provides investment banking services, such as strategic advisory services and capital markets products; merger and acquisition, equities capital market, debt capital market, debt advisory and restructuring, and fund placement services; and institutional equity sales and trading, equity research, equity derivatives and index options, convertible bonds, event driven sales and trading, and portfolio and electronic trading, as well as provides custody, clearing, and prime services. Further, the company offers institutional fixed income sales and trading, fixed income research, public finance, and municipal trading services; and proprietary trading and investment activities. Additionally, it provides underwriting, market-making, trust, and discount services, as well as a cloud-based financial market. The company serves high-net-worth individuals and families, corporate executives, public and private businesses, institutions and corporations, governments, financial sponsors, and domestic and international investors. The company was founded in 1881 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Oppenheimer Holdings, Inc. is a small-cap financial services business with a $972M market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $184M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 42% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.2) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Operating margins 16% below sector median — a cost disadvantage the moat cannot hide
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: 30 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 13% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 16pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.50x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 82% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 0.88, it moves roughly with the market.
About $11.7M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $85.09 (margin of safety -7%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 83%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $59.81 to $124 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/FCF 5.3 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 23% above its 10-year median.
The price implies 13.7% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.66).
It converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 15% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.8% over 3 years, 6.4% over 5 years and 5.8% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 86.3% on average.
own: Insiders own 42.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 43%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.1% (0.3% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 30 consecutive years, though it has been cut 16.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 3,009 employees, each generates about $544K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 3.9% a year.
That works out to $61K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.5M (16x revenue per employee).
